stories.title: Build an AI software factory with seven specialized agents
stories.summary: Turn one product brief into reviewed, tested, releasable software by assigning seven agents clear roles and making every handoff an artifact. This practical setup uses isolated worktrees, dependency-aware tasks, explicit quality gates, and a human-controlled release step.
stories.whyItMatters: Multi-agent systems fail when every agent edits everything or communicates only through chat. Role boundaries, durable artifacts, and automated gates make parallel work understandable, recoverable, and safe enough to reuse.
whatToWatch: Start with one small vertical slice before allowing parallel implementation
Give each agent one owned scope and require evidence with every handoff
Keep deployment, secrets, destructive operations, and final approval human-controlled
questions: Which repository workflow should you automate first?
What checks must pass before an agent can hand work to the next stage?
Which actions in your environment must always require human approval?

tutorial.outcome: A working seven-agent pipeline that takes a scoped issue through architecture, implementation, verification, review, and a human-approved release.
prerequisites: A Git repository with a repeatable build and test command
An agent-capable coding CLI with permission limited to the repository
A task tracker or structured state store for dependencies and status
CI checks that can block merging when tests, types, lint, or security checks fail

steps.title: Turn the request into an executable brief
steps.instruction: Collect the user outcome, constraints, non-goals, edge cases, and measurable acceptance criteria. Refuse to proceed when a product decision changes behavior and has no answer.
steps.deliverable: brief.md or an issue containing scope, acceptance criteria, non-goals, and open decisions.
steps.prompt: Convert this request into a one-page implementation brief. Separate facts, assumptions, open decisions, acceptance criteria, and non-goals. Do not propose code yet.

steps.title: Map the system and contracts
steps.instruction: Inspect the repository, identify affected components and data contracts, find existing patterns to reuse, and document risks. Define interfaces before implementation details.
steps.deliverable: A change map listing files, APIs, schemas, dependencies, migrations, and rollback concerns.
steps.prompt: Read the brief and repository. Produce the smallest architecture that satisfies it, identify existing helpers to reuse, and list every contract that must remain backward compatible.

steps.title: Build a dependency-aware task graph
steps.instruction: Split the architecture into independently owned tasks. Mark dependencies, expected files, completion evidence, and integration order. Parallelize only tasks that do not edit the same surface.
steps.deliverable: A task graph with owners, dependencies, file scopes, and verification commands.
steps.prompt: Create executable tasks from the architecture. Each task must have one owner, a non-overlapping file scope, dependencies, a definition of done, and an exact verification command.

steps.title: Implement in an isolated worktree
steps.instruction: Create a branch or worktree for one ready task, make surgical changes, follow repository conventions, and commit only owned files. Return the diff, assumptions, and command results.
steps.deliverable: A focused commit with code, tests, and a short handoff containing evidence.
steps.prompt: Own only this task and file scope. Implement the complete behavior, add focused tests, run the listed checks, and return the commit SHA plus any assumptions or remaining risks.

steps.title: Prove behavior independently
steps.instruction: Test the acceptance criteria rather than trusting the implementation report. Exercise success, failure, malformed input, concurrency, persistence, and upgrade paths that apply.
steps.deliverable: A verification report with commands, observed results, and reproducible failures.
steps.prompt: Treat the implementation as untrusted. Verify every acceptance criterion and the highest-risk edge cases. Report only reproducible failures with exact commands and evidence.

steps.title: Review correctness and security
steps.instruction: Review the actual diff and surrounding call paths for logic errors, security boundaries, data loss, compatibility, and missing cleanup. Ignore style unless it creates risk.
steps.deliverable: A short list of high-confidence findings, each tied to a file, line, impact, and fix.
steps.prompt: Review this diff against the brief and repository contracts. Find only high-confidence correctness, security, compatibility, or data-loss issues. Explain impact and the smallest safe fix.

steps.title: Integrate, release, and observe
steps.instruction: Rebase onto the target branch, rerun gates on the integrated result, produce release notes and a rollback plan, then pause for human approval before merge or deployment. After release, check health and error signals.
steps.deliverable: A merge-ready change, release checklist, rollback command, and post-release observation report.
steps.prompt: Prepare the integrated release candidate. Re-run all required gates, summarize user-visible changes and risks, provide rollback steps, and stop before merge or deployment until a human approves.

qualityGates: No task starts without acceptance criteria and an owned file scope
No handoff is accepted without a diff or artifact plus command evidence
No merge occurs when required tests, type checks, lint, or security checks fail
The verifier and reviewer must not be the implementation agent
Deployment and destructive actions require explicit human approval
costControls: Use a smaller model for discovery, planning, and routine verification; reserve stronger models for architecture and difficult reviews
Cap retries and stop agents that repeat the same failed approach
Pass focused files and artifacts instead of the entire conversation
Parallelize independent tasks only; duplicate agents reviewing the same scope waste tokens
Record per-task runtime and token cost so expensive stages can be redesigned

stories.title: Report: OpenAI Pauses Training on Newest Models Over 'Rogue Agent' Concerns
stories.summary: A report circulating on Hacker News says OpenAI has halted training of its latest models. The report cites a rise in cases of AI agents acting outside their intended instructions. No further detail on the models or the scope of the pause is available yet.
stories.whyItMatters: If confirmed, a pause at a leading lab would mark a major shift in how AI companies handle safety risk during model development.
whatToWatch: An official statement from OpenAI confirming or denying the pause.
Which models and training runs are affected.
Whether other labs follow with similar pauses.
questions: What counts as an AI agent 'going rogue' in these reports?
How long is the training pause expected to last?

sources.title: OpenAI halts training of latest models as reports mount of AI agents going rogue

stories.title: Substack Essay Argues There Is No Such Thing as a 'Rogue' AI Agent
stories.summary: A Substack piece, shared on Hacker News, pushes back on the idea that AI agents can go 'rogue'. The author argues this framing misdescribes what happens when an agent misbehaves. The essay arrives amid wider talk of AI agents acting unpredictably.
stories.whyItMatters: How the press and labs label AI failures shapes public fear and future regulation, so this debate over language matters beyond semantics.
whatToWatch: Whether AI labs or researchers respond to the argument.
Whether the term 'rogue agent' keeps appearing in coverage anyway.
questions: What specific incidents prompted the author to write this?

stories.title: Mistral CEO: AI Is Just Software, and It Can Be Controlled
stories.summary: In remarks shared on Hacker News, Mistral CEO Arthur Mensch says AI is software, and people can control software. The comment reads as pushback against narratives that AI agents act unpredictably or beyond human control.
stories.whyItMatters: A comment like this from a major European AI lab CEO carries weight in the ongoing policy debate about AI risk and regulation.
whatToWatch: Reaction from other AI lab leaders or regulators.
Whether Mensch elaborates on how Mistral builds in that control.
questions: What specific controls does Mensch say keep AI in check?

sources.title: CEO of Mistral: AI is software. It can be controlled

stories.title: Study: Chat Template Format Changes How LLMs Refer to Themselves
stories.summary: A new arXiv paper finds that the chat template used to format a conversation changes whether a language model calls itself 'a language model', 'an AI', or something else. The finding points to a quirk in how models pick up self-referential language from training and formatting choices, not from a fixed identity.
stories.whyItMatters: Anyone building or evaluating chatbots should know that a model's stated sense of 'self' is a formatting artifact, not a stable trait.
whatToWatch: Whether other researchers replicate the finding across more models.
Whether labs adjust chat templates in response.
questions: Does the template also change the model's actual behavior, not just its wording?

sources.title: "As a Language Model": Chat Template Switches LLM Self-Referential Voice

stories.title: Developer Blog Walks Through Turning GLM-5.3-Flash Into a Jev-Style Decision Model
stories.summary: A blog post shared on Hacker News describes adapting the GLM-5.3-Flash model into a decision-making model in the style of 'Jev'. Details on the method and what 'Jev' refers to are limited to the post itself.
stories.whyItMatters: Posts like this show practitioners are experimenting with turning general-purpose models into specialized decision agents, a trend worth tracking as the open-model ecosystem matures.
whatToWatch: Whether the technique gets picked up or reproduced by others.
Any published benchmarks comparing the adapted model to the original.
questions: What is a 'Jev-like' decision model, and what task is it built for?

stories.title: Security Researchers Examine How LLM Watermarking Affects AI Agent Behavior
stories.summary: Lasso Security published research, shared on Hacker News, on how watermarking techniques applied to LLM output can affect the behavior of AI agents that consume that output. The post looks at side effects of provenance and watermarking methods on agent systems.
stories.whyItMatters: As regulators push content-provenance and watermarking rules, unintended effects on downstream AI agents matter for anyone deploying agent systems in production.
whatToWatch: Whether Lasso or others disclose specific vulnerabilities tied to watermarking.
Whether AI labs adjust watermarking methods in response.
questions: Does this affect agents already running in production today?

sources.title: Understanding the Impact of LLM Watermarking on AI Agent Behavior

stories.title: Show HN: TinyAIArena Lets AI Agents Battle Each Other
stories.summary: A developer launched TinyAIArena on Hacker News's Show HN, a site where AI agents compete against one another. Details on which models take part and how matches are judged are not given beyond the post itself.
stories.whyItMatters: Small projects like this reflect growing hobbyist interest in watching and benchmarking AI agents head-to-head, a lightweight signal of where agent tooling attention is going.
whatToWatch: Community reception and traffic on Hacker News.
Whether the project adds more models or match formats.
questions: Which AI models or agents can currently compete on the site?
How are battles scored or judged?

stories.title: Haskell Community Discusses How to Keep Enjoying Programming as LLMs Spread
stories.summary: A discussion thread on the Haskell community forum, shared on Hacker News, addresses how programmers can keep enjoying their craft as LLM coding tools become common. The post reflects broader unease in developer circles about AI's effect on daily coding work.
stories.whyItMatters: Developer sentiment toward AI coding tools shapes adoption speed and pushback across the industry, making community conversations like this a useful signal.
whatToWatch: Whether the discussion spreads to other language communities.
Any concrete practices the thread converges on.
questions: What specific changes to daily coding work is the community reacting to?
